item.title: Node Running in Piz Palü
item.dc:creator: Andrius
item.content:encoded:
For most of HOPR’s history, running a node has meant something fairly passive and research focused. You staked wxHOPR, you kept a machine online, and you were paid for relaying cover traffic sent by the HOPR Association’s own nodes. The cover traffic was there to keep the mixnet busy and to test the protocol under load, and the rewards were there to keep nodes online until there was something real to relay.

That is about to change. HOPR v5 is out, nodes are moving to the Piz Palü network, and Gnosis VPN launches in Q4. For the first time, people will be paying to send their own traffic through the network. That changes what a node is for, what it needs to be good at, and how the HOPR Association and node runners work together.

At the same time, HOPR Association needs to shift focus from building and maintaining support tooling to better focus on protocol improvements. The massive shift in AI ability and availability in the past year means it’s now feasible for community members to contribute technically in ways that were unthinkable when HOPR launched.

This post goes through those changes. Running a node is becoming more interesting, and we think most people who have run nodes through the quiet years will like where we’re going.

Where the rewards come from

Under the previous model, a node’s income came almost entirely from incentive cover traffic, and eligibility depended on how much wxHOPR sat in your Safe. The traffic existed to reward stakers. That was the right design for a research network with no users yet, and it kept hundreds of nodes online through several protocol generations. During that time, network throughput has scaled over 1000x thanks to the work of the protocol engineers. That’s now enough to support actual VPN traffic.

With v5 there are two sources of rewards.

The first is cover traffic, which still exists but in a much different shape. Instead of a steady trickle sized to your stake, the Association’s cover traffic nodes send short, fast bursts to eligible relays. A relay qualifies by being reachable and having enough open, funded outgoing channels, which is the same thing the routing cares about, and it is paid per packet for the burst like any other traffic. The details are in our cover traffic post.

But by far the most important is real traffic. When a Gnosis VPN user opens a connection, their packets are routed through relay nodes chosen by the client, and every relay is paid with a ticket for every packet it forwards. This is the income the protocol was designed around from the beginning: Proof of Relay and probabilistic payments exist so that relays can be paid for work without anyone learning whose traffic they carried. As VPN usage grows, rewards grow too.

Stake will still matter, but in a different way. Thanks to the new probing traffic, every v5 node continuously measures the links around it, partly by sending packets to itself the long way round through two or three relays. Those relays cannot tell a probe from any other packet and are paid for it in the usual way. Your node pays for the probes it sends out of its own channels and is paid for the probes everyone else routes through it, so across the network the probe payments roughly cancel out.

Nodes are constantly making assessments about the state of the network and the quality of nodes around them. Stake will be a factor in these quality assessments, because well funded nodes are much more likely to stay online. So a node with a healthy Safe balance is much more likely to be assessed as high quality, and therefore much more likely to be chosen in routes and receive rewards.

In all cases, what pays is forwarding packets, and which nodes get packets to forward is decided by how well they perform.

The bar has gone up

We would like running a HOPR node to be possible for as many people as possible, and that is still the goal, but there is no getting around the fact that the requirements have moved. The v5 docs ask for four CPU cores, 4 GB of RAM and an uplink that can handle 10 Mbit/s in both directions. The v3 minimum was two cores and 2 GB.

The reason is what the node is now doing. A cover traffic burst arrives at around 10 Mbit/s and has to be relayed onward at the same rate. VPN traffic arrives whenever a user sends it, at whatever rate they send it. Probing adds a steady background of packets in both directions. A node that falls behind drops packets, and in v5 dropped packets are noticed: every node scores the links it measures and routes around the ones that perform badly, so a struggling node is chosen less and less often, and the peers that opened channels to it will eventually close them.

The v5 requirements are still within reach of a small home server or a modest VPS, and a node that meets them with room to spare has every chance of being chosen often. What we are asking is that you take them seriously. Good nodes are what make the network reliable and useful.

A different relationship with the Association

The other change is in what you should expect from us.

Over the years the HOPR Association has built a lot of software around the node itself: the Staking Hub for onboarding and managing Safes, the Admin UI, dashboards, and a succession of onboarding flows. A web application like the Staking Hub is a serious engineering commitment to build and a continuing one to maintain, and every hour spent on it is an hour not spent on the protocol, on the client, or on the things Gnosis VPN needs to work.

With v5 removing the network registry and the minimum stake, the Hub is no longer needed for onboarding, and it will be wound down. The Association will concentrate on the things only we can do: the protocol itself, the reference implementation, and the tooling you need to run a node from the command line. That means hoprd, the node daemon; hopli, the CLI for identities, funding and Safe setup; the Admin UI for day-to-day management over the node’s REST API; and documentation that covers all of it. The network dashboard stays for now. Everything we build remains free and open source, as it always has been.

We will always be here, but we do need to node runners to start being more proactive and independent. There will be fewer web apps built to smooth over a single step, and less of the Association acting as the first line of support for every configuration question. Node runners on Dufour have, between them, far more operational experience with HOPR than any team could, and v5 is the point at which we would like that experience to carry more of the load.

Build your own tools, and share them

This is the part we are most looking forward to.

The distance between “I would like a tool that does X” and “I have a tool that does X” has shrunk enormously over the past two years. A node runner who wants a script that watches channel balances and tops them up, a dashboard that graphs their node’s scores over time, an alert when a peer closes a channel, or a one-command setup for their particular hosting provider can now have it in an afternoon, with an AI assistant doing most of the typing. The node’s REST API exposes everything the Admin UI shows and a good deal more, there is a TypeScript SDK for it, and the node exposes metrics you can scrape.

We encourage you to do exactly this. We also encourage you to point your AI tools at our material directly. Our documentation, the RFCs that specify the protocol, and the source repositories are all public, and an assistant that has read them will answer most questions about running a node better than a search through Discord history. We have started publishing agent skills that package the RFCs for this purpose, and where we can, we will keep writing and structuring what we publish so that it is as useful to a machine reading it as to a person.

What we would ask is that you think beyond your own node. Most node runners have the same needs. If you have built something that solves a problem for you, it almost certainly solves it for a few hundred other people, and publishing it costs very little more than keeping it to yourself.

Where to find things

The place to look for tools, and the place to put yours, is Awesome HOPR on GitHub. It already lists the official software above, along with the Ansible role, Homebrew tap, Dappnode package and Kubernetes operator for the people who need them, plus the indexer, the smart contracts, the session explorer and a Wireshark dissector for anyone who wants to see what a HOPR packet looks like on the wire.

Anything the Association recommends will be on that list. Community tools belong there too, and the contributing guide explains how to add one. If you have written something useful, open a pull request. If you are looking for something, check there before you build it.

What to do now

If you already run a node, migrate it to v5 and Piz Palü following the migration guide, and check whether your hardware meets the new minimums with room to spare. If you are new, start a node. There is no registration and no minimum stake, so all you need is a machine and some wxHOPR for channels.

Then watch how your node performs. Keep it reachable, keep its channels funded, and if you find yourself wanting a tool that doesn’t exist yet, build it and tell us about it on Discord.

The network that Gnosis VPN users connect to later this year is the one node runners build over the next few months. We think it is going to be a good one.

item.title: Network Probing
item.dc:creator: Andrius
item.content:encoded:
When you send a HOPR packet your node must select the whole route in advance. If part of that route fails, the packet won’t be delivered, so it’s important to choose well. A poor choice can lead to lost packets, lost payments, and disrupted service for users.

The network is permissionless, decentralized and constantly changing, so it’s hard to get an idea of what the network looks like beyond your immediate neighbours. You can read the list of payment channels on-chain to understand what funded routes are possible, but that doesn’t tell you about the nodes connected to these channels.

The way we dealt with this until now was the heartbeat. A node would ping the peers it knew about and keep a running score for each of them. So a node had a reasonable idea of which peers were there, but no idea how fast they were or whether they forwarded packets, and nothing was known about nodes more than one hop away, which in a multi-hop route is most of them.

So in v5 the heartbeat has been upgraded to probing. This greatly improves nodes’ knowledge of the network, by sending a constant (low) stream of real traffic. This post explains what probing does, what it costs, how other nodes now rate yours, and what that means for your channels.

What your node sends now

Pings haven’t gone away. In every probing round your node sends each of its connected peers a short message with a random number in it and waits for the same number to come back. That gives it the round-trip time and tells it whether the peer is answering. The ping goes directly, with no relay and no ticket, and the peer can see it’s a probe.

The new part is that your node also sends packets to itself via a multi-hop path. It picks a route through two or three other nodes that ends up back where it started and sends a normal HOPR packet round it. If the packet comes back, every link on the loop was working, and the time it took is the delay of the whole loop. Your node already knows how long each neighbour takes to answer a ping, and it sends a lot of loops through overlapping groups of nodes, so with some subtraction it can work out roughly how much delay each node is adding.

None of the relays on a loop can tell they’re carrying a probe. Like all HOPR traffic, packets are indistinguishable. Ordinary traffic counts as well: a reply that comes back through a SURB is evidence that every link out and back was working.

By default probing happens once a minute. Each round sends one ping to every connected neighbour, plus up to 100 loops through two relays and up to 100 loops through three. A well-connected relay will reach both of those caps.

How other nodes rate you

Each node keeps a score for every link it knows about, including the link from each of your neighbours to you. The score comes from the proportion of recent probes across the link that succeeded and from how long they took. Latency is scored in bands. Anything up to 75 ms round trip gets full marks. From 76 to 125 ms the score is 0.7, from 126 to 200 ms it’s 0.3, and above that it’s 0.15. The success rate and the latency score are multiplied together, so a link that answers every probe but takes 150 ms to do it ends up at 0.3.

The other change since the heartbeat is that there is no cut-off any more. When a node needs a route it lists the candidate paths, multiplies together the link scores on each one, and draws a path at random with the odds weighted by the results. A slow or lossy node isn’t excluded from the draw, it just comes up less often, and because the scores multiply, one bad link makes a whole route unlikely. Even a link measured as dead keeps a very small chance of being tried, so the node notices if it comes back to life. There is also a mild preference for better-funded paths, which stops mattering once a channel holds about 100 wxHOPR.

You can’t see how other nodes score you, because nodes never share their scores; a node’s scores would reveal which routes it has been considering. The only indications are indirect ones, like whether your peers keep their channels to you open and whether traffic keeps coming.

What it costs

The heartbeat didn’t cost anything to run. Probing does, because loops are real packets and your node pays for them the same way it pays to send anything else. The ticket it attaches is worth the per-hop price multiplied by the number of relays on the loop. At the current price of 0.00001 wxHOPR per hop, a full round of 100 two-relay loops and 100 three-relay loops adds up to 0.005 wxHOPR, and at one round a minute that’s 7.2 wxHOPR a day.

That money goes to other relays. Each loop your node sends pays the nodes it passes through, and each loop they send through your node pays you, so across the network probe spending moves between relays rather than leaving the system. A relay also keeps one hop-price from every packet it forwards for anybody else, and cover traffic costs nothing to relay because your node is its last hop. A relay with good scores from its peers gets routed through more and covers its probe costs without difficulty; one with poor scores pays the same and gets routed through less.

What this means for your channels

The channel lifecycle strategy that comes with v5 uses these scores. It opens channels to peers that are connected and scoring well, and closes channels to peers whose scores have dropped below a threshold, who haven’t been seen for a day, or whose channel has run dry. The same strategy on other nodes is doing this to you: score well with a node and it opens a channel to you and sends traffic through you, score badly for long enough and it closes the channel again after a grace period.

The default is to fund each outgoing channel with 150 wxHOPR, open five to begin with, and grow towards 30 as the strategy finds good peers. That covers the probe spending for months between top-ups, it’s beyond the point where funding makes any difference to path selection, and it’s 50 above the cover traffic eligibility floor of 100 per channel, so a run of winning tickets against one channel won’t knock you out of the eligible set. Since a balance only moves when a ticket wins, and a winning ticket is worth 2.5 wxHOPR, it goes down in steps rather than steadily, and a channel is better judged over weeks than days.

What to do

There isn’t a great deal to do. Your node’s own API shows you what it has measured about every peer it’s connected to, and the troubleshooting page in the docs explains how to open it in a browser. The settings that control probing are in the configuration reference, but you shouldn’t change from the defaults (especially as we’ll be tuning numbers regularly). Your node needs to be reachable from outside, because a node that can’t be dialled scores nothing with anybody, so check the IP address and port it announces. Make sure your node meets the minimum specs and latency is as low as you can get it. Channel management is best left to the strategy. Keep your Safe topped up, because the various random factors in the protocol can lead to balance volatility in the short run.

Probing is the first step towards decentralized cover traffic: real multi-hop traffic from every node that serves to make the network more useful as well as more private.

item.title: PIX: How Exits Get Paid
item.dc:creator: Melissa Guenthardt
item.content:encoded:
HOPR v5 includes a new protocol called PIX, the Protocol for Incentivization of eXits. It solves the problem of how to pay the exit nodes that carry Gnosis VPN traffic out of the mixnet and onto the Internet, without the payment revealing who the user is. This post explains how PIX works and what it means for Gnosis VPN users and node runners. A technical write-up will follow separately.

The problem

HOPR pays relay nodes per packet. A relay earns a ticket for handing a packet on to the next node in the route, but what about the exit? There is no next node after it, so no ticket is created and no reward earned.

That’s bad, but it’s actually the smaller half of the problem. In Gnosis VPN, the exit is responsible for serving requested content to the user. When the exit sends the reply back, it becomes the sender of those packets, and in HOPR the sender pays the relays. But it gets worse. Replies are most of the traffic. A request for a web page is a few hundred bytes, but the page itself is megabytes. So an exit goes unpaid for what it receives and pays for what it sends, and what it sends is nearly everything. Obviously these are mismatched incentives.

So far the exits have been run by the project, so we’ve been able to bear the cost. But for Gnosis VPN to become a network of independently run exits, including exits on home connections, the people running them have to be paid.

The trouble is that all the obvious ways to do this break the privacy the mixnet provides. A subscription paid to a central account means somebody has a list of every user. A direct payment from user to exit lets the exit tie a payment to a session, and an account to a person.

PIX borrows the idea behind proof of relay: make each party’s payment depend on the other’s behaviour. The user pays for the data the exit delivers, but the exit cannot collect before delivering. The user cannot take the money back once delivery has started. And nothing on the network or on the blockchain links a user to an exit or a session.

How it works

Payment is settled in fixed chunks of data rather than for a whole session. When a session opens, the client’s entry node and the exit agree on a chunk size: some number of megabytes that the exit will deliver back to the user. A long session is a series of chunks, each agreed before the previous one finishes so the connection never pauses. The direction that counts is data flowing back to the user, because that is the direction the exit has been paying for.

A deposit neither side can spend

For each chunk the two nodes construct a fresh address together. The private key for that address is in two parts: the exit chooses one and the entry node the other, and each sends the other only what it needs to compute the address, never its half of the key. The entry node then deposits the price of the chunk to that address. Neither side can withdraw it alone.

Earning the key by delivering

The entry node splits its half of the key into a large number of shares using a secret sharing scheme. Any one share, or any handful of them, reveals nothing. Enough of them together reconstruct the key exactly.

Replies through the mixnet can only be sent using SURBs (single-use return blocks), the pre-built single-use return envelopes the user’s node supplies. PIX attaches one encrypted share to every SURB, and the exit can only decrypt it once the first relay on the return path has acknowledged the packet sent with that SURB. One packet delivered back towards the user, one share earned.

The number of shares needed is matched to the chunk size. When the exit has delivered the agreed amount of data it has enough shares to rebuild the user’s half of the key, combines it with its own, and withdraws the deposit. A few spare shares cover packet loss, paid for as part of the chunk.

Why nobody can cheat

The exit cannot collect without delivering, because shares only unlock when the next relay confirms receipt. If the user sends junk shares, the exit checks each one against commitments the user made when the address was set up, and the first bad share ends the session with the deposit still locked. If the user leaves the connection open but stops using it, the exit keeps sending keep-alive packets, each spending a SURB and earning a share, until the chunk completes.

Keeping payments off the record

The per-chunk addresses never appear on the chain. They live inside a privacy pool, a shared contract that users pay into and exits withdraw from. A user tops up the pool once with a round sum, chosen in advance, that says nothing about how it will be spent. The chunk deposits are then made inside the pool, each to a fresh address that receives one deposit and is never used again, and each for the standard price of a chunk, so there is nothing on the chain that reads as “this user paying this exit”. When an exit withdraws, it proves that it is entitled to the funds without revealing which deposit it is spending. The chain shows that a user put money into the pool and that an exit took money out, and nothing about which deposit paid which exit.

We’ve partnered with Curvy to build the pool. Curvy is a privacy protocol for public blockchains, and the version that runs inside hoprd was adapted for PIX so that an exit can see a payment arrive before it holds the key to spend it. Curvy have written up their side of the design in their own post.

What it means for Gnosis VPN users

You pay for the data that comes back to you, in chunks, out of the funds in your Gnosis VPN account. The client handles the deposits automatically. A few things follow from the design.

First, exit choice is extremely important. Once you choose an exit, you will prepay for a certain quota of data, which you will then redeem over the course of a session. So you shouldn’t randomly click between exits or you’ll quickly drain your balance. The UI will ensure that you can’t easily accidentally switch between exits.

An idle connection is not free. If you stay connected without using the tunnel, the exit fills the current chunk with keep-alive packets, so an open connection costs a slow trickle of chunks until you disconnect.

Disconnecting and reconnecting starts a new chunk, and the one you were in is paid in full. In return you get a new pseudonym, new keys and a fresh payment address, with nothing carried over from the old connection. This is important, because it prevents the exit from learning too much about you as time passes. But it does mean you need to keep an eye on your session quota.

What it means for relays

If you run a relay node, there’s nothing to configure. Your node sees HOPR packets with tickets on them as before. What changes is the volume: since PIX closes the incentive gap in the network, we would expect to see a lot more organic traffic and hence a lot more tickets earned.

What it means for exits

If you want to run an exit, PIX is what makes it worth doing. With v5 and the exit registry, anyone can be an exit. If you’d like to learn more, get in touch with us.

At first, PIX parameters will be standardised. Although exits are free to modify them, the client will not, so any attempt to deviate from the network standard will result in a failed connection. As PIX is battle tested and more independent exits join, restrictions in the client will be loosened and exits will be able to set different quotas and prices.

item.title: HOPR Piz Palü Release
item.dc:creator: Andrius
item.content:encoded:
HOPR v5 is out. It’s the release that removes the network registry and the minimum stake, and it moves HOPR nodes onto a new network, Piz Palü, that is built for Gnosis VPN. Node runners can migrate today.

Gnosis VPN launches in Q4 2026. It will be the first consumer product built on HOPR at this scale, with users paying to send real traffic through the network. Everything in this release is in service of that.

If you want to run a HOPR node, there is now nothing standing in your way.

Anyone can run a node

The network registry and the minimum stake were introduced when controlling the size of the network was important. They let us bring nodes on gradually while the protocol was still being developed and tested in production. The network has grown out of that stage. Gnosis VPN needs a larger network, and there is no good reason to make prospective node runners register or clear a stake threshold before they can contribute to it.

Running a HOPR node no longer requires registration. There is no waitlist, no network registry, no Staking Hub onboarding and no minimum stake. You create a Safe for your node, fund it, and start.

Because onboarding no longer goes through it, the Staking Hub will be shut down. If you ran a node on the previous network, your old Safe will still be yours after that, but the Hub is the easiest place to withdraw your wxHOPR from it, so do that as part of your migration (see below) and don’t leave it too long. We will monitor migration and keep it running for a few weeks at least, but don’t leave it until the last minute.

What else is new in Piz Palü?

A lot has changed under the hood since Dufour and hoprd v3. These are the big ones node runners will notice:

Blokli

Until now every HOPR node has indexed the HOPR smart contracts itself, which meant finding a reliable Gnosis Chain RPC provider, waiting for the initial sync, and dealing with RPC outages and rate limits as a routine part of running a node. In v5 that work moves to Blokli, a dedicated indexer that watches the HOPR contracts and provides nodes with the on-chain state they need. HOPR runs a Blokli instance for the Piz Palü network, and nodes connect to it by default, so there is no initial sync to sit through and no RPC provider to configure. Blokli is open source, so if you’d rather not depend on ours you can run your own against your own RPC endpoint.

Channels look after themselves

Payment channels are how a node gets paid and how it pays the next hop. Earlier releases had separate strategies for opening channels and topping them up, and plenty of node runners managed them by hand. v5 ships with a single channel lifecycle strategy, enabled by default, that handles the whole job. It opens channels to peers that your node can reach and that perform well, funds them, tops them up before they run dry, and closes them when a peer’s quality drops or when the channel is drained. Channel capacity is now expressed as an amount of data (a channel funded for a gigabyte, say) rather than a token amount, and the node works out the wxHOPR needed from the current ticket price and winning probability. You can still manage channels by hand through the Admin UI or the API if you prefer.

Dynamic routing

v5 includes new probing mechanisms and a path-finding model in which every link between nodes carries a score built from probe results and latency, and from the round trips of real traffic. Routes are drawn at random, weighted by those scores, so a node that is reachable, fast and reliable is chosen more often, and one that drops packets is chosen less often rather than being cut off outright. Return paths are now spread across different relayers as well. Taken together, this is what makes the point below about running a node well more than a request: how much traffic reaches your node now depends on how your node performs.

Network probing

The HOPR network is constantly changing, large, and set to grow even bigger. To help deal with this, nodes now send out probing traffic according to a strategy in order to build an accurate picture of the network and help to build reliable routes via useful nodes. This means there will be a steady outflow of tokens from your node, but it will be compensated by an inflow of tokens from other node’s probing traffic. You may see some fluctuations in balance, particularly in the early stages of this new network, but it should settle down. Cover traffic and VPN traffic will of course act to mitigate this. Network probing also acts as cover traffic: a steady stream of packets from all nodes that provides a blanket of privacy.

Burst cover traffic

Incentive cover traffic stays in place, but instead of just blasting out rewards for stake, it will reward nodes based on their connectivity, funding, and power. Bursts of cover traffic will be sent out in cycles to all nodes with the requisite number of funded channels. Nodes with poor specs may be unable to process these bursts of data and rewards will drop accordingly. Nodes missing channels or funding won’t even get the chance to try.

What running a node means now

For the last several years, most HOPR node runners have experienced the network through cover traffic. Keep a node online, keep the right channels open and funded, relay cover traffic, collect the rewards.

But running a HOPR node is evolving into operating infrastructure that other people depend on. When Gnosis VPN launches, HOPR nodes will relay real traffic from people using a VPN. That places much higher requirements on all of your nodes: they need to stay online. They need to be reachable. They need funded channels. Above all, they need to relay traffic reliably. If not, a user will notice it in their VPN connection.

If you run a node, we want you here. But we want you here to run it well. Gnosis VPN will depend on the network underneath it, and every node on that network has a job to do.

If you want to learn more about the changes to cover traffic and probing traffic, please read our dedicated blog: https://medium.com/hoprnet/cover-traffic-on-hopr-piz-pal%C3%BC-8023ea67bdbd.

What to do

If you already run a HOPR node, you need to migrate it by the 27th of October. This is more than a version bump: your node moves from the Dufour network to Piz Palü, which means creating a new Safe and node module and moving your wxHOPR across. Before you start, redeem your outstanding tickets and close your incoming channels, and back up your identity file. The migration guide walks through every step for Docker, Docker Compose and Dappnode: https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/migrate-node-from-v3

If you’re new to HOPR, start a node. Setup instructions are in the HOPR docs: https://docs.hoprnet.org docs.hoprnet.org

Gnosis VPN

Gnosis VPN is a VPN built on the HOPR mixnet. It lets people use HOPR’s privacy infrastructure through a product they already understand.

The nodes that come online over the coming months will form the network Gnosis VPN users connect to when the product goes live in Q4 2026.

If you want early access to Gnosis VPN, you can join the waitlist at the website: https://vpn.gnosis.eth.limo

What’s next

Relay nodes are one part of carrying VPN traffic. When a user’s traffic reaches the end of its route through the HOPR mixnet, it has to leave the mixnet and reach the open internet. That is the job of a new kind of node: an exit node.

Exit nodes need to be paid for the traffic they deliver, without the payment revealing which user or VPN session the traffic came from. PIX is the mechanism we have developed to make that possible. It comes into use alongside Gnosis VPN, and it deserves more explanation than fits in a release post, so we’ll publish a dedicated piece on how it works soon.

Running an exit will involve more requirements than running a relay node, and those requirements are still being finalized. All of the development is happening in public, though. If you want to follow the work or start digging into the implementation now, you can find it here: https://github.com/gnosis/gnosis_vpn-server

We’re looking forward to seeing more people running HOPR nodes, and to getting the network ready for what comes next. Gnosis VPN will depend on the nodes that are online, reachable and reliable when it launches. If you’re running one, keep it healthy and keep paying attention. The network we build now is the network people will soon be using.

item.title: HOPR Basics: PIX
item.dc:creator: Melissa Guenthardt
item.content:encoded:
HOPR Basics, part 14 of 14. First published October 2026. The full index is at the end of the article.

Over the last three episodes we’ve built up a picture of how Gnosis VPN works on top of HOPR: an exit carries your traffic out of the mixnet onto the public Internet, it sends its replies back in pre-built, single-use envelopes called SURBs, and a session turns all those packets into a connection your computer can use.

We also kept running into the same loose end. Every relay node in the chain is paid for its work through proof of relay and tickets, but the exit, which does the most work of all, is paid nothing. The ticket for the final hop is worth zero, and that’s deliberate: proof of relay pays a node for handing a packet on to the next one, and after the exit there is no next one. Worse, when the exit sends your data back, it’s the exit that pays the relays on the return route, and the data coming back is nearly all of the traffic. The exit ends up out of pocket for serving you.

The protocol that fixes this is called PIX, which stands for Protocol for Incentivization of eXits. It’s new, and some of its settings are still being tuned, but the mechanism itself is settled.

What We Need From an Exit Payment

The incentives episode set out why HOPR couldn’t just have users pay a subscription into a central pot: whoever ran the pot would know who every user was. Paying exits has the same constraint, plus a few of its own.

The user should pay the exit for the data it delivers, but the exit shouldn’t be able to collect until it has actually delivered. The user shouldn’t be able to take the money back once the exit has started working for it. And the exit should learn nothing about the user in the process. An exit that could link payments to sessions could link sessions to people, which would undo all the work of putting a mixnet between them.

This is very similar to the problem proof of relay solved. There, we needed two neighbouring nodes to be unable to cheat each other, and the answer was to make each one’s payment depend on the other. PIX uses the same approach, stretched out across a whole session.

A Deposit Neither Side Can Open

When a session opens with PIX, the exit and the user’s entry node agree on an amount of data: a block of so many megabytes that the exit will deliver back to the user. That direction is the one that matters, because it’s the direction the exit has been paying for. Call it a cycle. Everything that follows happens once per cycle, and a long session is just a sequence of cycles. Paying in cycles means neither side ever has more than one cycle’s worth committed to the other, and as we’ll see at the end, it also keeps the payment trail short.

For each cycle, the two nodes jointly create a fresh deposit address. The key that controls the address is made of two parts. The exit chooses one part and keeps it secret, and the entry node does the same with the other part. Each sends the other just enough information to work out the address, but not the other half of the key. The result is an address that neither of them can empty on their own. (These are called stealth addresses, and we’ll come back to why that matters.)

The entry node then deposits the price of the cycle into that address. The money is now committed. The user can’t claw it back, because the user doesn’t have the exit’s half of the key. But the exit can’t take it either, because it doesn’t have the user’s half.

So how does the exit get hold of the user’s half?

Earning the Key One Packet at a Time

The answer is a technique called secret sharing. The entry node takes its half of the key and splits it into a very large number of pieces. Any single piece, or even a few thousand of them, tells you nothing about the key. But collect enough of them and the key can be reconstructed exactly. It’s like a jigsaw where the picture only appears once nearly all the pieces are in place, and no single piece shows you anything on its own.

Remember from the return path episode that the exit can only send data back to the user using SURBs, the return envelopes the user supplies. PIX attaches one piece of the key to every SURB.

The piece isn’t handed over for free, though. It’s locked, and the exit can only unlock it once the first relay on the return route confirms that it has received the packet the exit sent using that SURB. So the exit gets one piece of the key for each packet of data it actually sends back towards the user.

The number of pieces needed to rebuild the key is matched to the size of the cycle. Once the exit has delivered the agreed amount of data, it has gathered enough pieces to reconstruct the user’s half. It combines this with its own half, and now it controls the deposit address. It sweeps the funds into its own account, and the cycle is complete. The next cycle is agreed before the current one finishes, so there’s no pause in the connection.

A little slack is built in. Packets get lost on real networks, and a lost packet means a lost piece, so the entry node sends a few more pieces than the bare minimum. That surplus is paid for as part of the cycle, in the same way you pay for insurance whether or not you claim on it.

Why Nobody Can Cheat

Let’s look at the ways this could go wrong.

The exit can’t collect without delivering, because the only way to get key pieces is to send packets back, and each piece is released only when the next relay acknowledges the packet. The user can’t withdraw the deposit, because half the key belongs to the exit.

What if the user sends junk instead of real key pieces? The pieces can be checked, in batches, against commitments the user made when the address was set up, and the first failed check ends the session. All the user achieves is to forfeit a deposit they’ve already made.

Finally, if the user leaves the connection open but stops using it halfway through a cycle, the exit isn’t left with a half-earned deposit forever. It can keep sending keep-alive packets to the user, each one spending a SURB and earning a piece, until the cycle completes. So an idle connection isn’t free: it costs a slow trickle of cycles for as long as it stays open.

Keeping Payments Private

Everything above happens between the two nodes, inside the mixnet. The one place it touches the outside world is on-chain, where the deposit goes in and the exit’s withdrawal comes out, and we saw in the tickets and payment channels episode how much a public blockchain can give away.

Two things keep PIX from leaking. First, every cycle uses a brand new address that exists for that one deposit only, so nothing on the chain reads as a payment from a particular user to a particular exit for a particular session. Second, the deposit doesn’t go straight from the user’s account to that address. It goes through a privacy pool: a shared on-chain pot that users pay into and exits withdraw from, designed so that an outside observer can’t match a withdrawal to the deposit that funded it. The chain shows that a user put funds into the pool and that an exit took funds out, but not which deposit paid which exit, or for which session.

This is the same rule we met in the sessions episode, applied to payments. A single deposit covering a whole evening’s browsing would be one address holding one revealing amount for as long as the evening lasted. Cycles break that into a series of shorter payments, each to an address that has never been used before and never will be again, with the pool hiding which deposit funded which withdrawal. The money moves on at the same pace as the pseudonyms and the routes.

With PIX in place, every node that handles Gnosis VPN traffic is paid for the work it does, and none of them learns who the user is.

item.title: HOPR Basics: Sessions
item.dc:creator: Melissa Guenthardt
item.content:encoded:
HOPR Basics, part 13 of 14. First published October 2026. The full index is at the end of the article.

We now have the two halves of a conversation through the mixnet: packets going out, each on its own route, and SURBs coming back, each on its own route too. But we still don’t have a connection. Your web browser and your operating system don’t think in packets and reply envelopes. They expect something that behaves like a wire: you open it, data flows in both directions in the right order, and eventually you close it.

HOPR provides this with a session. In this episode we’ll look at how a session works, and then at a question the earlier episodes skipped over: how long should one last?

Opening a Session

A session is a two-way connection between an entry node and an exit, carried entirely over the mixnet. In Gnosis VPN the entry node is the small HOPR node built into the client on your device, and the exit is the one you picked from the list.

It starts with a handshake. Your entry node sends the exit a request to open a session. The request says what the exit should do with the data it receives (the target: forward it to a particular address and port, over TCP or UDP) and which features the session should use. The exit checks that it serves that target and has capacity for another session, and confirms. From then on, every packet belonging to the session is labelled with its session ID so both sides know which conversation it’s part of. If either side goes quiet for too long the session is closed, so while it’s open, both ends send occasional keep-alive packets.

In Gnosis VPN the target is the exit’s own WireGuard server. The session acts as a pipe, and the WireGuard tunnel runs through it. (There are actually two sessions: a control session, used to register your WireGuard key with the exit and keep an eye on the exit’s health, and the main one that carries the tunnel itself.)

Fitting a Stream into Packets

The mixnet episode explained why every HOPR packet is exactly the same size: if packets had different sizes, an observer could track one through the network just by watching for its size. Unfortunately, a VPN tunnel produces a continuous stream of data, which somehow has to be made to fit.

So the session protocol chops the stream into frames, splits any frame too big for a single HOPR packet into numbered segments, and sends each segment as its own packet. The receiving end collects the segments and puts them back in order to reassemble the frame. If this sounds familiar, it’s because the Internet itself splits data into numbered packets in much the same way.

Sessions come in two flavours. A reliable session behaves like TCP: the receiver acknowledges each frame and asks for any segments that went missing, and the sender retransmits them. An unreliable session behaves like UDP: packets are sent once, and if one is lost, it’s lost. That might sound worse, but it’s often what you want. The traffic inside the tunnel already handles its own ordering and loss recovery (that’s what TCP does, and WireGuard is built to run over a lossy connection), so wrapping it in a reliable session would mean doing the same work twice and adding delay for nothing. Gnosis VPN’s main tunnel uses an unreliable session.

Either way, each segment is still a normal HOPR packet. It takes its own route through the relay nodes and is mixed with everyone else’s traffic, generating proof of relay tickets at every relay hop just as in earlier episodes.

Anonymity Has a Half-Life

All of this makes a session sound like a pure convenience, a way of pretending that a lot of separate packets are a wire. But there’s a privacy cost, and it explains a lot about how Gnosis VPN is designed.

So what does stay the same for the life of a session? The routes are re-chosen for every packet, and the relays see nothing but encrypted packets passing through. But the exit sees the same pseudonym on every packet, delivers to the same WireGuard key, and watches one continuous stream of requests go out and replies come back. None of this identifies you, and each individual packet gives away almost nothing. Unfortunately, almost nothing is not the same as nothing, and over a long session it adds up.

Every action you take over a connection carries a small chance of leaking something that could be linked to something else: the timing of a request, the size of a response, a pattern of destinations that only one person would have. An observer who sees one of these learns very little, but one who can collect them from the same session for an hour has a lot more to work with. The exit is in the best position to do this collecting, and so is anyone watching traffic go in and out of the network and trying to match the two up.

You could say that anonymity has a half-life. When a session opens you’re as anonymous as you’ll ever be, with a new pseudonym, new keys and no history yet. From then on, the longer the session runs, the more an observer has to work with. (This is the logic of the dark forest: you’re safe as long as you keep moving and say as little as possible, and the longer you stay in one place, the more someone watching learns about where that place is.)

The way out is to leave, and come back as someone new. A HOPR session is designed to be disposable. Disconnecting and reconnecting costs a handshake, a few packets and (as we’ll see next time) a fresh payment cycle, and the new connection has a different pseudonym and a different WireGuard key, with nothing carried over from the old one. The clock restarts.

Change Your Connection to Privacy

Of course, this is a trade-off. A connection that never changed anything would be very convenient and terrible for privacy, and one that changed everything with every packet would be perfectly private and completely unusable. Sessions sit somewhere in between, and much of the design of Gnosis VPN comes down to keeping as much as possible moving while still handing your browser something that works.

The same idea comes up again and again. A conventional Internet connection is anchored to one thing, your IP address. Everything you do is tied to it, and a VPN only moves that fixed point from your address to the VPN provider’s. HOPR replaces it with things that keep moving: routes are chosen per packet, pseudonyms and keys last for one connection, and, as we’ll see next time, even the payments are broken into short cycles, each one paid to a fresh address. And on top of all that movement, sessions still manage to give you a connection that feels, from your side of the screen, basically unbroken.

Next time we’ll look at how an exit gets paid for all this, and why the payment protocol follows the same rule.

item.title: HOPR Basics: The Return Path
item.dc:creator: Melissa Guenthardt
item.content:encoded:
HOPR Basics, part 12 of 14. First published October 2026. The full index is at the end of the article.

Last time we introduced exits, the nodes that carry Gnosis VPN traffic out of the mixnet and onto the public Internet. We said the exit fetches what you asked for and sends it back to you, and moved on. But that last part hides a problem that took a lot of work to solve.

Everything in the earlier episodes was about moving one packet in one direction. You wrap a message in layers of encryption, send it off, and some time later it pops out at the far end. That’s fine for delivering a message to a friend. But almost nothing you do online is one-way. You ask for a webpage and the page comes back, and the page is usually a great deal bigger than the request: you send a few hundred bytes and receive a few megabytes. So most of the traffic in a VPN connection is actually flowing towards you.

Remember, the exit at the far end has no idea who you are. It knows your packets came from the last relay in the chain, and nothing else. So when it has a reply ready, where does it send it?

Replying to a Stranger

The anonymous routing episode used the analogy of a parcel of nested envelopes, each addressed to the next person in the chain. The sender builds the whole parcel, because only the sender knows the full route. That’s what keeps the route secret, but it’s also what leaves the exit stuck: it can’t build a parcel back to you when it doesn’t know where you are.

The solution is that you build the parcel for the return journey as well, and send it along with your request. HOPR calls these pre-built return parcels SURBs (single-use reply blocks). A SURB is a complete set of nested, encrypted routing instructions for a path from the exit back to your entry node, with the message left blank. The exit can’t read the instructions, so it has no way of telling where the parcel will end up, or even which relay comes after the first one. All it can do is put its reply inside and hand the whole thing to the first relay on the return route, and the mixnet takes it from there.

Every packet you send carries a short random pseudonym, and the SURBs you send carry the same one. That lets the exit file your SURBs under your pseudonym and pick the right ones when it replies to you rather than to someone else. When the reply arrives at your end, your entry node recognizes the pseudonym, unwraps the remaining layers and passes the data on. At the HOPR level, the pseudonym is the only name the exit has for you. It isn’t tied to your device or your location, and it doesn’t carry over to anything else you do.

As the name says, each SURB works exactly once. A second packet built from the same SURB would look like a repeat to the relays, which drop it. So once a SURB has been used, it’s thrown away.

Keeping the Exit Supplied

If every reply packet needs its own SURB, and most of a VPN connection is replies, then a download of a few megabytes needs thousands of SURBs. Sending one SURB with each request would never keep up, so your entry node has to keep the exit stocked. (Note that a SURB only tells the exit where to send a reply packet. The relays that carry it still expect to be paid, and it’s the exit, as the sender of that packet, who pays them. We’ll come back to this in episode fourteen.)

HOPR handles this with SURB balancing. Your entry node tucks SURBs into the packets it’s already sending, and when that isn’t enough it sends keep-alive packets containing nothing but fresh SURBs. It keeps an estimate of how many the exit has left (the exit reports its true level back every so often) and tries to keep the supply ahead of demand. Meanwhile the exit paces how fast it sends data to match the SURBs it has in hand. If the stock runs low it slows down, and if it runs out entirely it has no way to reply at all until more arrive.

This is one of the ways a connection through HOPR feels a little different from an ordinary one. The speed of a download depends on how fast the exit can fetch the data, and also on how fast your side can keep supplying the envelopes to send it back in. So a fast download needs a steady stream of upstream packets from you, even if you aren’t sending anything else.

Nothing Stays Still

There’s one more thing to say about SURBs, because it comes up again in the next two episodes. The route inside a SURB doesn’t have to match the route your request took, and it doesn’t have to match the route inside the next SURB either. Your entry node picks a route for each packet it sends, drawn at random from a shortlist of the best-performing routes it knows about, and it does the same for each SURB it builds. The exit sees a stream of reply envelopes and has no way to tell whether any two of them take the same route back.

So it’s a mistake to picture a connection through HOPR as a fixed line from you to the exit, with replies coming back along it. What you actually have is a swarm of individually routed packets in each direction, and the only constant is the pseudonym that lets the two ends keep track of which conversation they’re in. Next time we’ll look at how HOPR turns all those packets into something your computer can treat as a connection, and at why even the pseudonym shouldn’t be allowed to last too long.

item.title: HOPR Basics: Exits
item.dc:creator: Melissa Guenthardt
item.content:encoded:
HOPR Basics, part 11 of 14. First published October 2026. The full index is at the end of the article.

The first ten episodes of this series explained how the HOPR mixnet moves a packet of data from one person to another without anyone being able to see who is talking to whom. In those explanations, the person at the end of the chain was usually “your friend”: someone who, like you, runs a HOPR node and is waiting to receive your message.

That picture is accurate as far as it goes, but it leaves out almost everything people actually do online. When you load a webpage, stream a video or check your email, the thing at the other end is an ordinary server somewhere on the public Internet. It doesn’t run a HOPR node, and it has never heard of HOPR.

So for a mixnet to be useful as a VPN, someone has to stand at the edge of the network and carry your traffic across the gap, out of the mixnet onto the open Internet and back again. In Gnosis VPN, that someone is an exit.

The Last Node in the Chain

An exit runs a HOPR node, and like any node it relays other people’s packets. It also has a second job: it accepts connections from Gnosis VPN users and forwards their traffic to the public Internet. From the Internet’s point of view, the exit is where your traffic comes from.

When you connect, your device uses a lightweight HOPR node built into the Gnosis VPN client, and this acts as your entry to the network. The client picks an exit and opens a connection to it through the mixnet. That connection uses the same relaying and onion-style layers of encryption we described in the anonymous routing episode, and the same mixing we described in the mixnet episode.

Over that connection, your client sets up a standard WireGuard VPN tunnel to the exit. WireGuard is the same protocol used by many conventional VPNs, and it’s what your operating system actually talks to. All your device’s Internet traffic is wrapped in the WireGuard tunnel, the tunnel is carried inside HOPR packets, and the HOPR packets hop across the mixnet to the exit.

At the exit, the layers come off in reverse. The exit unwraps the HOPR packets, reassembles the WireGuard tunnel, decrypts it, and sends your request on to its real destination using the exit’s own Internet connection. The website you asked for sees a request coming from the exit’s IP address, in the exit’s country, and sends its reply back there. The exit wraps the reply up again and sends it back across the mixnet to you.

What the Exit Knows

After the metadata episode, the obvious question is what the exit gets to see.

It sees the same things any VPN server sees. It knows which websites and services you’re connecting to, because it has to in order to forward your traffic. If a connection isn’t separately encrypted (most of the web now is, via HTTPS, but not all of it), the exit can see the contents too. So far this is just the same as the server of a commercial VPN provider.

The difference is what the exit doesn’t know. A commercial VPN server sees your real IP address on one side and your destinations on the other, so using one really means trusting the company that runs it. An exit doesn’t see your IP address. Your packets arrive from the last relay node in the chain, and all the exit can tell about their origin is that relay’s address. Every packet in a connection carries a short random pseudonym so the exit can tell your connection apart from other users’, but the pseudonym isn’t tied to your device or your location. Nor is it tied to any other connection you make.

So the knowledge that a conventional VPN concentrates in one place is split up. The exit knows where your traffic is going, but has no idea who you are. The relay nodes know neither. Your entry node does know who you are, but it’s on your own device and it can’t see inside the tunnel. And because you can use different exits at different times, there isn’t a single party anywhere that can build up a profile of your activity.

How much of this protection you get depends on the route. Gnosis VPN sends traffic through the mixnet’s relay nodes before it reaches the exit, and the number of hops is a setting. More hops means more mixing and less chance of anyone correlating what goes into the network with what comes out. Unfortunately, it also means more latency. But with even one relay in the route, the exit never sees you directly.

Who Runs Exits?

Anyone with a HOPR node, a public IP address and a bit of configuration can run an exit. The node needs the Gnosis VPN server component installed alongside it, which manages the WireGuard side of things, and it needs to tell the HOPR software that it’s willing to forward traffic. By default a HOPR node refuses to act as an exit for anything at all. An operator has to opt in, and can say precisely which services they’ll forward to. A Gnosis VPN exit forwards only to its own VPN server, which in turn handles the general Internet.

Exits announce themselves on-chain in a registry, along with some information the operator chooses to publish, such as a name and a location. The Gnosis VPN client reads this registry to build the list of exits you can choose from. (The location is self-declared, so there’s no guarantee it’s accurate.)

Running an exit is a bigger commitment than running a relay node. A relay only ever handles encrypted packets it can’t read, and never talks to anyone outside the HOPR network. An exit is the public face of other people’s traffic. Websites see the exit’s address, so an operator who runs an exit from home is lending their home Internet connection to strangers. But this also has an upside. VPN blocking often works by refusing traffic from the IP ranges that belong to data centres, and connections from ordinary residential addresses are much harder to block. That’s why the aim is a network of exits spread across many homes and many countries, which would be very difficult to shut out.

Of course, operators need some say over what they carry. Exits can refuse connections they don’t want to serve, and the admission rules an exit applies are the operator’s decision.

Paying the Exit

There’s one more difference between an exit and a relay, and this one is a problem. The whole incentive system described in the proof of relay and tickets episodes pays nodes for passing a packet on to the next node. The exit is the end of the chain. There is no next node, so there’s no ticket worth anything for the final hop.

That’s only half of it. Once the exit has fetched what you asked for, it has to send it back to you, and in HOPR, sending data through the mixnet means paying the relays who carry it. So as well as going unpaid for your request, the exit has to pay out of its own pocket to deliver the answer. Intuitively it’s the user who should be paying for that, since the user is the one who wanted the data. As things stand, the exit loses twice.

And the second loss is the bigger one. Requests are small and responses are large. “Send me this page” is a few hundred bytes; the page itself, with its images and scripts, can be megabytes. The traffic the exit pays for is many times the traffic it carried for free.

So the exit does more work for the user than any relay node, since it runs the VPN server, fetches the data and sends it back into the mixnet, and the payment system, far from paying it, leaves it with the bill. That gap is filled by a separate protocol, and how it works depends on how replies find their way back through the mixnet. We’ll look at the return journey next time, and get to the payment protocol in episode fourteen.

item.dc:creator: Andrius
item.content:encoded:
With the release of HOPR v5, nodes will migrate to a new network: Piz Palü. Piz Palü radically changes how cover traffic works, to better support a network with live services, particularly Gnosis VPN. Minimum stake is gone, and with it the formula that paid each node a percentage of what it had locked in its Safe. In its place, cover traffic nodes send short bursts of real traffic through every node that meets a minimum threshold for open, funded payment channels. Just like “real” traffic, receiving and relaying these bursts will earn you rewards.

This post explains what has changed, why, and what you need to do. The v5 release post covers the migration itself; this one is only about cover traffic.

How it worked on Dufour

Cover traffic has always been paid the same way as any other HOPR traffic: a cover traffic node sends packets through your node, and each packet carries a ticket. What the old system decided centrally was how many packets you should get.

Until now, that number was based on your stake. To receive any cover traffic at all, a node needed at least 30,000 wxHOPR in its Safe, or 10,000 with a Network Registry NFT. Above 75,000 wxHOPR the stake was transformed so that additional tokens counted for very little.

The floor and the cap belonged to a permissioned network, where it made sense to limit who could join and to stop a few large holders taking the whole budget. Now HOPR is transitioning to a working network, where the main priority is high quality nodes to relay real users’ data.

Cover traffic on Piz Palu is changing to incentivize this. Cover traffic on Dufour will continue during the migration period, but will be reduced to zero over the next few weeks.

What counts now

On Piz Palü, a node is eligible for cover traffic when a cover traffic node can reach it and has sufficient well-funded payment channels.

Channels are what the network runs on. To forward a packet on to another relay, a node needs a funded channel to that relay, so a node with five funded channels is a node the network can route through, and a node with 50,000 wxHOPR sitting in a Safe and no channels is not. Making channels the test means the cover traffic budget goes to nodes that actually benefit the network.

We’re still tuning the cover traffic parameters, but for now the cover traffic nodes look for relay nodes with at least five open outgoing payment channels, each holding at least 100 wxHOPR. Stake in the Safe, Safe balance and location play no part. In addition to favouring useful nodes, this also massively reduces the cost to enter the network.

Don’t fund to the minimum, though. When your node forwards traffic on a multi-hop path, it pays the next hop out of its channel to that node. This will temporarily reduce your channel balance and could make you ineligible for cover traffic. We’d suggest at least 150 wxHOPR per channel. The default channel funding strategy in your node will already do that for you.

Bursts

How is cover traffic distributed? There are five cover traffic nodes on Piz Palü. Each one runs in rounds. At the start of a round it takes every node it considers eligible, shuffles them in an order that can’t be predicted from outside, and then works through the list, opening a one-hop session through each node in turn and sending a burst of traffic through it. It doesn’t wait for one burst to finish before starting the next.

A burst currently lasts 10 seconds at 30 Mbit/s relayed. Every packet crosses your node twice, once on the way to the destination and once on the way back, and you earn a ticket each time, so your node forwards about 12.5 MB per burst and receives tickets for all of it. As always, whether a ticket is a winner depends on the ticket winning probability, and the amount paid per ticket depends on the ticket price. Both are subject to tuning as we continue to test the network.

The rounds are timed so that, averaged across the five cover traffic nodes, every eligible node gets a burst about once every 20 minutes. The step between bursts shrinks as more nodes become eligible, so the interval each node sees stays roughly constant whatever the network size.

Nothing else is calculated. There is no yearly target per node, no stake-weighted share of a budget, no transformed anything. If your node relays a burst, it has the tickets to show for it. If it was unreachable when its turn came, it was skipped for that round and the next round starts over.

This is a test

The values above are a starting point. Five channels and 100 wxHOPR per channel are the first eligibility settings we are trying, and the burst size and interval were chosen so that a reasonable number of nodes can be served from a budget we can sustain. As the network grows and we see how nodes behave under bursts, we expect to adjust them, and we will say so when we do. The per-node figures above are what the system pays under today’s settings.

The figures may change, but the mechanism won’t. Eligibility will be based on funded channels, rewards will be tickets on packets your node actually relayed, and the cover traffic nodes will keep working through every eligible node in turn.

HOPR needs high quality nodes

Under the old model a node could earn its full allocation on very modest hardware, because the traffic arrived as a slow trickle spread across the day. A burst is different. For 10 seconds your node is receiving, processing and forwarding around 860 packets a second, counting both directions, and because the five cover traffic nodes schedule independently, two bursts can land on it at once.

A node that can’t keep up drops packets, and every dropped packet is a ticket it doesn’t get. It also looks worse to its peers: other nodes score the peers they connect to and close channels to the ones that perform badly, which takes a slow node further out of the paths that pay. Under Gnosis VPN, the same shortfall shows up as a bad connection for whoever is routed through it.

The minimum for a relay node is four CPU cores, 4 GB of RAM and 5 GB of disk. When choosing a VPS plan for a node you expect to be paid, ideally give it headroom above that, and make sure the uplink can carry 10 Mbit/s in both directions without choking. VPS services generally offer lower performance cores than you would get on your own hardware.

Cover traffic is only part of earnings

Cover traffic is changing to support a new network filled with real users. If your node is eligible to receive cover traffic, it will also receive real traffic. So while rewards from cover traffic will likely drop, earnings from real traffic should significantly increase for all high quality nodes. It’s obviously impossible to calculate rewards in advance, but even relatively modest testing generated over 2TB of real data in a month, all of which relayers were paid for.

What to do

If you already run a node, migrate it to the Piz Palü network by following the guide in the release post, and once it is running, check that it has at least five open outgoing channels with 100 wxHOPR or more in each. If it does, cover traffic will find it. Cover traffic will continue on Dufour for the next weeks to support the migration, but will be tapered during that time and fully switched off afterward.

If you run into issues, reach out to us on Telegram or check the docs at https://docs.hoprnet.org
